moves.source: Lina Bo Bardi, converting an old drum factory into the SESC Pompeia leisure center and her 'poor architecture' stance
moves.move: Keep what already stands and is loved, add the minimum new thing beside it, and let what is plain carry the character.
moves.asks: What is already here that is worth keeping intact, and what is the smallest addition that brings it to life?

moves.source: Horace, Ars Poetica, advising the poet to plunge 'in medias res' and not begin with the egg
moves.move: Open at the moment where things are already happening and let the backstory arrive only when it is needed.
moves.asks: What is the earliest part I assume I must include that could be skipped, so we start where it gets interesting?

moves.source: Wen Tong (praised by Su Shi), the Song-dynasty idea of having 'complete bamboo in the chest' before painting the first stroke
moves.move: Study and absorb the subject until you can see the whole finished form inwardly, then execute in one fluent pass.
moves.asks: Can I see the whole thing clearly in my head, and if not, what do I still need to look at before the first stroke?

moves.source: Leonardo da Vinci, Treatise on Painting, on finding landscapes and battles in stained walls and mixed stones
moves.move: Stare at random mess and let your mind pull shapes out of it, then develop the ones that appear.
moves.asks: If I looked at a pile of random marks, scraps or noise related to this, what forms would I start to see?

moves.source: Hannah Hoch, Dada photomontages cut from magazines and mass media (Cut with the Kitchen Knife)
moves.move: Cut existing finished pieces apart and reassemble the fragments into something that comments on where they came from.
moves.asks: Which ready-made things could I cut up and recombine, and what new meaning appears in the seams?

moves.source: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Sower, built by extending present trends forward and her 'positive obsession' notes
moves.move: Take a trend already happening, follow it faithfully several decades forward, and design for the world it produces.
moves.asks: If the current trend around this simply continued for thirty years, what would be normal then, and what would people need?

moves.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction'
moves.move: Replace the story of the spear-hunter's conflict with the story of the bag: gather, hold and relate many things in a container.
moves.asks: What if this were designed as a bag that holds many small things together rather than a single heroic thrust?

moves.source: Yayoi Kusama, her Infinity Nets and polka-dot Infinity Mirror Rooms, obsessive repetition of one motif
moves.move: Pick one small unit and repeat it past the point of reason until the repetition becomes the subject and the boundaries dissolve.
moves.asks: What single element could I repeat a thousand times, and what appears when quantity takes over?

moves.source: Diebedo Francis Kere, the Gando Primary School in Burkina Faso built from local clay bricks by the villagers themselves
moves.move: Design the building method around the materials and labor of the community, so that making the thing builds the people who will use it.
moves.asks: What material and skills does the community already have, and how could building it together be part of the design?

moves.source: Mierle Laderman Ukeles, 'Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!' and her work shaking hands with sanitation workers
moves.move: Treat upkeep, repetition and the unglamorous tasks that keep things running as the main creative subject instead of an afterthought.
moves.asks: What would this look like if the maintenance and daily upkeep were the point and the invention were secondary?

moves.source: Hayao Miyazaki, discussing 'ma', the deliberate pauses in action, in conversation with Takeshi Kitano
moves.move: Put deliberate empty beats between the busy parts, because the quiet gives the busy parts their meaning.
moves.asks: Where could I insert a pause with nothing happening, and what would the surrounding action gain?

moves.source: Abbas Kiarostami, his statement that he favors 'half-made films' that the audience completes (Close-Up, Taste of Cherry)
moves.move: Leave a deliberate gap in the work so the person experiencing it has to complete it with their own mind.
moves.asks: What part could I leave unfinished on purpose so that the user finishes it and owns it?

moves.source: Jacob Lawrence, painting the 60 panels of The Migration Series together, one color at a time across all panels
moves.move: Work on every piece of a series at the same time and advance one variable across all of them before moving to the next, so the whole stays coherent.
moves.asks: What one variable could I advance across every part at once so the whole stays unified as it develops?

moves.source: Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, writing parts for the particular sound of individual band members like Johnny Hodges and Cootie Williams
moves.move: Compose for the specific strengths and quirks of the actual people who will carry it out, not for generic roles.
moves.asks: Who are the actual people or tools involved, and what idiosyncratic gift of theirs could the design be written around?

moves.source: Arvo Part, his tintinnabuli style, a strict two-voice system devised after years of silence and study of plainchant
moves.move: Strip the work down to one simple, rigorously applied rule, and let a plain beauty come from following it exactly.
moves.asks: If I could keep only one rule and apply it with complete strictness, what would it be and what would remain?

moves.source: Bharata Muni, the rasa theory of the Natyashastra, in which a work is built to evoke one dominant flavor of feeling
moves.move: Choose the single dominant emotion the audience should savor and let every element be selected to deepen it.
moves.asks: What one feeling should the person be left with, and which parts do not serve it?

moves.source: Zhuangzi, the story of Cook Ding carving an ox (Zhuangzi ch. 3)
moves.move: Stop cutting where it is solid, and feel for the natural gaps so the blade passes through spaces that are already there.
moves.asks: Where are the natural joints in this problem where almost no force is needed?

moves.source: Laozi, the wheel hub, clay pot and room windows (Daodejing ch. 11)
moves.move: Treat the empty space as the thing you are designing, because the pot, wheel or room is useful only through what is not there.
moves.asks: What emptiness must I deliberately leave so that this becomes usable?

moves.source: Confucius, the rectification of names (Analects 13.3)
moves.move: Check whether each thing is called what it truly does, and fix the name or the thing until they agree.
moves.asks: Does each part here actually do what its name claims, and what would it be called if named honestly?

moves.source: Wang Yangming, the unity of knowing and acting (Instructions for Practical Living)
moves.move: Treat knowledge not yet acted on as not yet really known, and let the doing be the test of the understanding.
moves.asks: What is the smallest real action that would show me what I actually know?

moves.source: Nagarjuna, the catuskoti or four-cornered negation (Mulamadhyamakakarika)
moves.move: Refuse to stop at 'is' or 'is not', and examine 'both' and 'neither' before accepting the framing.
moves.asks: What answer sits outside both sides of the either/or I am stuck in?

moves.source: Eihei Dogen, Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo Kyokun)
moves.move: Handle the humblest ingredient with the same full care as the finest, and make a meal from whatever the kitchen actually has.
moves.asks: What would make the plainest material I have the centre of the whole thing?

moves.source: The Buddha, the poisoned arrow parable (Culamalunkya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 63)
moves.move: When wounded, pull the arrow out first and defer the questions about who shot it and from where.
moves.asks: Which interesting question can I park so that I deal with the thing causing harm right now?

moves.source: Jain anekantavada and syadvada, the many-sidedness of truth, later often illustrated by the blind men and the elephant
moves.move: Qualify every claim with 'from this standpoint' and list the standpoints that make each partial truth hold.
moves.asks: From which viewpoint is each rival claim true, and what whole do they sketch together?

moves.source: Rabia al-Adawiyya, as told in Attar's Sufi hagiography: the water and torch to put out hell and burn paradise
moves.move: Remove both the reward and the punishment and see what is still worth doing for its own sake.
moves.asks: If every payoff and penalty vanished, what part would people still love?

moves.source: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), the Floating Man thought experiment (Kitab al-Shifa)
moves.move: Strip away every outside input and sense, then see what is still there that you cannot deny.
moves.asks: With every added feature and context removed, what remains that is essential?

moves.source: Al-Ghazali, The Deliverance from Error (al-Munqidh min al-Dalal)
moves.move: Study each rival school thoroughly, then live inside the most promising one before judging it.
moves.asks: Which competing approach have I only read about and not actually tried from the inside?

moves.source: Simone Weil, attention as the rarest form of generosity (Waiting for God; letter to Joe Bousquet)
moves.move: Suspend the urge to solve, hold the thing in full attention without effort, and let its true shape come to you.
moves.asks: What do I notice if I look at this long and silently before trying to fix anything?

moves.source: Hannah Arendt, thinking without a banister (Denkgelander, interviews and Men in Dark Times)
moves.move: Put aside the received frameworks and categories, and think from the particular events themselves.
moves.asks: Which inherited framework am I leaning on, and what do I see if I let go of it?

moves.source: G. E. M. Anscombe, actions are intentional under a description (Intention, 1957)
moves.move: Redescribe the same act in several ways, because what it is, and what it is for, depends on the description chosen.
moves.asks: Under what other description is this same activity something quite different?

moves.source: Aristotle, the four causes (Physics II.3)
moves.move: Explain a thing four ways: what it is made of, what form it takes, what brings it about, and what it is for.
moves.asks: Which of material, form, maker or purpose have I left unexamined?

moves.source: Marcus Aurelius, the view from above (Meditations, books 7 and 9)
moves.move: Lift your viewpoint high over the scene, over crowds and centuries, and see the matter at its true scale.
moves.asks: How does this look from far above, across a long span of time and many people?

moves.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, family resemblances and 'don't think, but look' (Philosophical Investigations section 66)
moves.move: Instead of defining a category, lay out many real instances and note the overlapping similarities that actually connect them.
moves.asks: Looking at real examples, what do they truly share, and is there no single common essence?

moves.source: John Rawls, the veil of ignorance (A Theory of Justice)
moves.move: Design the arrangement without knowing which position within it you will occupy.
moves.asks: If I did not know who I would turn out to be here, what would I build?

moves.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, the eternal recurrence thought experiment (The Gay Science, section 341)
moves.move: Imagine living this choice again, unchanged, innumerable times, and keep only what you would affirm.
moves.asks: Would I choose this again, endlessly, exactly as it is?

moves.source: Mary Midgley, philosophy as plumbing (Utopias, Dolphins and Computers)
moves.move: Treat a persistent trouble as a leak that points to a hidden pipe, and trace it to the buried assumption rather than mopping the symptom.
moves.asks: Where is the hidden pipe that this leak is coming from?

moves.source: Kwasi Wiredu, conceptual decolonization (Cultural Universals and Particulars)
moves.move: Translate a key concept into another language and watch which hidden assumptions fail to carry across.
moves.asks: Which word am I using that smuggles in an assumption, and what breaks when I say it in another tongue?

moves.source: The Hatata inquiry attributed to Zera Yacob, said to be written after retreating to a cave (Ethiopia, 1667; its authorship is debated)
moves.move: Withdraw from authority and examine each received teaching using only reason and the evidence of creation.
moves.asks: Which inherited rule still stands once I examine it alone, with only reason as my guide?

moves.source: Gloria Anzaldua, la frontera and the mestiza consciousness (Borderlands/La Frontera)
moves.move: Live in the border between two worlds and build from the tolerance for contradiction that crossing demands.
moves.asks: What new thing can only exist where these two contrasting worlds meet?

moves.source: Robin Wall Kimmerer, the Honorable Harvest, Potawatomi teachings (Braiding Sweetgrass)
moves.move: Take only what is given, never the first or the last, never more than half, and return something in kind.
moves.asks: What is the least I need to take here, and what do I give back?

moves.source: Vine Deloria Jr., place over time in American Indian thought (God Is Red)
moves.move: Organise understanding around particular places and what happened there, instead of around a timeline of progress.
moves.asks: What if this were arranged around a specific place and its stories rather than around a sequence?

moves.source: Julian of Norwich, the hazelnut vision (Revelations of Divine Love)
moves.move: Hold the whole of the matter as something small enough to cup in the palm, and find what holds it together.
moves.asks: If the entire thing were a hazelnut in my hand, what would hold it together?

moves.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, interbeing and the cloud in the sheet of paper (The Heart of Understanding)
moves.move: Look into the thing until you find everything it depends on that is not itself.
moves.asks: What non-obvious things, people and conditions are inside this that I normally don't count?

moves.source: Archimedes, The Method (balancing shapes on an imagined lever to discover results before proving them)
moves.move: Find the answer first by a loose physical analogy you would never publish, then worry about rigor afterwards.
moves.asks: What crude, hands-on stand-in could show me the answer now, before I make it defensible?

moves.source: Eratosthenes measuring Earth's circumference from shadow angles at Syene and Alexandria
moves.move: Take one cheap measurement from two separated places and let simple geometry infer the thing you cannot reach.
moves.asks: Which two vantage points, each easy to read, would let me deduce the unreachable quantity?

moves.source: Liu Hui's commentary on the Nine Chapters (circle area by ever-finer polygons)
moves.move: Approximate the curved, messy whole by many straight simple pieces, and keep refining until the error is bounded and small enough.
moves.asks: What simple pieces, repeated finely enough, would stand in for this complicated shape?

moves.source: Ibn al-Haytham, Book of Optics (controlled experiments with the camera obscura)
moves.move: Turn the favored explanation into a setup where nature can say no, and trust only what survives repeated trials.
moves.asks: What arrangement would visibly fail if my favorite idea were wrong?

moves.source: Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Jabr (restoring and balancing equations)
moves.move: Apply the same operation to both sides until the unknown stands alone in a standard form with a known recipe.
moves.asks: What can I add or remove on both sides of this problem until only the unknown is left?

moves.source: Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays (repeated nightly sightings of the pole star, which showed it is not exactly at the celestial pole)
moves.move: Record the same observation at regular intervals long enough to learn that the reference you treated as fixed is not quite where you assumed.
moves.asks: What am I treating as fixed that a long, regular log would show is moving?

moves.source: Gregor Mendel's pea-plant crosses (seven sharp binary traits, thousands of counted offspring)
moves.move: Choose variables that come in clean either/or forms and count a large number of cases so a hidden ratio shows itself.
moves.asks: Which crisp, countable feature could I tally over many cases to reveal the pattern under the mess?

moves.source: Ignaz Semmelweis comparing the two Vienna maternity clinics' death rates
moves.move: Set side by side two near-identical settings with different outcomes and list every difference until one survives.
moves.asks: Where does a near-twin of this situation turn out differently, and what actually differs between them?

moves.source: Florence Nightingale's coxcomb charts of Crimean War mortality
moves.move: Redraw the data so the person with power over the decision cannot look at it without seeing the cause.
moves.asks: How could I draw the evidence so the decision-maker feels the answer at a glance?

moves.source: Ada Lovelace, Notes on the Analytical Engine (suggesting it could compose music)
moves.move: Describe what the machine does in general terms, stripped of its first use, then ask what else those operations could act on.
moves.asks: If I describe my tool's basic operations without naming its original subject, what new subjects can it work on?

moves.source: Emmy Noether's theorem linking symmetries to conservation laws
moves.move: Ask what you can change without changing the result, because whatever stays constant under a change is the thing you can rely on.
moves.asks: Which transformations leave this unchanged, and what does that tell me must be preserved?

moves.source: Marie and Pierre Curie isolating radium and polonium from pitchblende by tracking radioactivity
moves.move: Pick one measurable trace and follow it through each successive separation, always keeping the fraction that carries the most signal.
moves.asks: What single measurable signal can I track while splitting this into smaller parts?

moves.source: Jagadish Chandra Bose's crescograph, magnifying plant movements about ten thousand times
moves.move: When the response you care about is too faint to perceive, invent an instrument that amplifies it until it becomes undeniable.
moves.asks: What device could magnify the tiny effect until I can watch it directly?

moves.source: Maryam Mirzakhani's habit of drawing on huge sheets of paper while working on hyperbolic surfaces
moves.move: Spread the problem across a large surface and draw it, accepting being lost for a long time until a path appears.
moves.asks: How would the problem look if I drew it huge and wandered around inside the picture?

moves.source: Katherine Johnson hand-verifying NASA's electronic computer trajectories before John Glenn's flight
moves.move: At the moment of highest stakes, independently recompute the automated answer by a different route before trusting it.
moves.asks: Where would a second, independent calculation of the automatic result be worth the effort?

moves.source: Grace Hopper handing out lengths of wire to show how far light travels in a nanosecond
moves.move: Hand people a physical object that makes an abstract quantity something they can hold.
moves.asks: What object could I put in someone's hand to make this abstraction tangible?

moves.source: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring (tracing pesticides link by link through soil, water and food chains)
moves.move: Follow a substance or decision through every link of the chain it enters, to see who ends up paying for it.
moves.asks: If I follow this through each link it touches, where does it surface that I did not expect?

moves.source: Vera Rubin's galaxy rotation curves, measured out to the faint outer regions
moves.move: Measure the edges everyone ignores, since the center behaves as expected and the edge exposes the missing piece.
moves.asks: What happens at the far edge of this system that nobody has bothered to measure?

moves.source: Gertrude Elion's rational drug design at Burroughs Wellcome (exploiting biochemical differences between diseased and healthy cells)
moves.move: Study how the target differs from everything you want to spare, then build the intervention to exploit exactly that difference.
moves.asks: What is chemically or structurally different about the thing I want to hit versus the things I must not harm?

moves.source: Alice Ball's injectable chaulmoogra oil esters for leprosy treatment
moves.move: Keep the ingredient that works and change its form until it can be delivered the way people actually need it.
moves.asks: What already works but is stuck in a form nobody can use, and how could I reshape it?

moves.source: George Washington Carver's Tuskegee bulletins on crop rotation and on uses for peanuts and sweet potatoes
moves.move: Start from what poor local people already grow or throw away, and invent uses until the surplus becomes the resource.
moves.asks: What is abundant, cheap and unwanted around here, and what could it become?

moves.source: Elizabeth Blackburn studying telomeres in the pond ciliate Tetrahymena
moves.move: Find a strange organism or case where the feature you want to understand is so exaggerated it is easy to see.
moves.asks: Where does this phenomenon appear in an extreme, overgrown form that makes it easy to study?

moves.source: Tu Youyou rereading Ge Hong's fourth-century handbook while isolating artemisinin
moves.move: Reread an old recipe literally, because the modern method may have broken a detail the old one quietly specified.
moves.asks: What does the oldest instruction for this say that the current method silently ignores?

moves.source: Ahmed Zewail's femtosecond laser pulses to photograph chemical reactions mid-step
moves.move: To understand something too fast to follow, take a rapid series of snapshots shorter than the event itself.
moves.asks: How could I freeze the middle of the process by sampling it faster than it changes?

moves.source: C. V. Raman asking why the sea is blue on a ship voyage, with a pocket spectroscope
moves.move: Take an everyday 'why' that adults stopped asking and investigate it with whatever tools are in your pocket.
moves.asks: What ordinary thing here has an answer nobody checked, and what could I check it with right now?

moves.source: Shinya Yamanaka's reduction of 24 candidate factors to four for induced pluripotent stem cells
moves.move: Start with every plausible ingredient together, then remove them one at a time to see which are truly required.
moves.asks: If I throw in everything first and subtract one piece at a time, which pieces turn out essential?

moves.source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (the imitation game)
moves.move: Replace a question that cannot be settled with a game whose outcome anyone can observe.
moves.asks: What observable test could stand in for this argument about definitions?

moves.source: Jocelyn Bell Burnell noticing 'a bit of scruff' on miles of chart recorder paper, discovering pulsars
moves.move: Treat the small recurring oddity that everyone filters out as the main finding, and go back to it.
moves.asks: What small repeating anomaly am I dismissing as noise?

moves.source: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman's modified nucleosides for mRNA that evades immune alarm
moves.move: When a promising idea is rejected, find the one signal that sets off the rejection and disguise just that part.
moves.asks: What exactly triggers the rejection, and can I alter only that trigger?

moves.source: Dorothy Hodgkin's X-ray crystallography structures of penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin
moves.move: Gather many partial flat views of the same object from different angles, then patiently assemble them into its true shape.
moves.asks: Which different angles of view, each incomplete, could be combined into the full structure?

moves.source: Mary Anning interpreting coprolites and bezoar stones from the Lyme Regis cliffs
moves.move: Read what a creature leaves behind, such as waste, traces and stomach contents, to reconstruct how it lived.
moves.asks: What does this thing leave behind that shows how it behaves when no one is watching?

moves.source: Kikunae Ikeda isolating glutamate from kombu broth and naming umami
moves.move: When an experience fits none of your existing categories, isolate its cause and give it its own name.
moves.asks: What do people keep experiencing that my categories cannot describe, and what is the pure cause?

moves.source: Max Theiler's yellow fever 17D vaccine, weakened by serial passage through mouse and chick tissue
moves.move: Make a dangerous thing safe by repeatedly passing it through a different environment until it no longer thrives in the original.
moves.asks: What alien environment could I grow this in, over many generations, until it loses its harm but keeps its use?

moves.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War: win by shaping the ground before the battle
moves.move: Spend your effort changing the terrain, supplies and expectations so the outcome is nearly decided before any direct contest begins.
moves.asks: What could I change about the situation beforehand so the hard part becomes easy or unnecessary?

moves.source: Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah: group cohesion (asabiyyah) and the rise-and-decay cycle of dynasties
moves.move: Treat anything people build as having a life cycle driven by how tightly its members are bound, and design for the third generation, not the founders.
moves.asks: What binds the people involved here, and what happens to that bond once the originals are gone?

moves.source: Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons: studying how real communities already manage shared resources
moves.move: Before inventing a rule or system, study how the people who actually share the scarce thing already govern it, and build on what works.
moves.asks: Who already lives with this problem, and what informal arrangements have they invented that survive?

moves.source: Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities: 'eyes on the street'
moves.move: Arrange things so ordinary, self-interested daily use produces the watchfulness and care that would otherwise need a dedicated guard.
moves.asks: How can the everyday users of this thing generate its upkeep and safety just by being there?

moves.source: Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil, frequency-hopping patent for torpedo guidance
moves.move: Defend or protect a signal by constantly switching channels on a pattern that only the two cooperating ends share.
moves.asks: What if this kept changing in step with a partner, on a pattern an outsider can't predict?

moves.source: Wangari Maathai, Green Belt Movement: paying women per surviving seedling
moves.move: Reward the lasting result rather than the act, and put the work and the payoff in the hands of ordinary local people.
moves.asks: What would I pay for if I only rewarded what is still alive a year from now?

moves.source: Ela Bhatt, founding SEWA, the union and bank for self-employed women
moves.move: Gather the people the system treats as invisible into a collective and give them their own institution, so they set the terms.
moves.asks: Who is working here without a seat at the table, and what organization of their own would change their bargaining power?

moves.source: Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of the Oppressed and his literacy method of 'generative words'
moves.move: Build the lesson out of the learner's own charged vocabulary and daily world, so learning the thing is also naming their reality.
moves.asks: Which words or objects already carry weight for this person, and can the whole structure grow from them?

moves.source: Christopher Alexander, A Pattern Language
moves.move: Describe a solution as a named pattern: the competing forces, and the arrangement that resolves them, then compose a whole from small patterns.
moves.asks: What forces are pulling against each other here, and which proven arrangement settles them?

moves.source: Genrich Altshuller, TRIZ: resolving technical contradictions by separation
moves.move: State the problem as two demands that fight each other, then refuse the compromise and separate them in time, space or scale.
moves.asks: What two things do I want that contradict, and could they hold at different moments, places or sizes?

moves.source: Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System: the andon cord that lets anyone stop the line
moves.move: Make every defect halt work at the moment it appears so it is fixed at its source while the cause is still visible.
moves.asks: What would it look like if any problem stopped everything until its cause was understood?

moves.source: Al-Jazari, Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices: water-driven automata and clocks
moves.move: Replace a repeated human action with a mechanism run by a flow already available nearby, with a cam or float deciding each step.
moves.asks: What is already flowing past this problem that could do the repeating work for free?

moves.source: Amartya Sen, the capability approach in Development as Freedom
moves.move: Judge a solution by what people become able to do and be with it, not by the resources or features it hands them.
moves.asks: After this exists, what can a person do that they could not do before?

moves.source: Kate Raworth, Doughnut Economics: a social foundation and an ecological ceiling
moves.move: Define the floor that must be met and the ceiling that must not be crossed, then search for designs inside the ring between them.
moves.asks: What is the minimum this must deliver, what is the limit it must not exceed, and what lives in between?

moves.source: Herbert Simon, bounded rationality and satisficing
moves.move: Write down in advance what counts as good enough, then take the first option that clears it instead of hunting for the best.
moves.asks: What is my stated aspiration level, and which option already meets it?

moves.source: Thomas Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict: focal points for coordination without communication
moves.move: When parties must line up without talking, choose the option that stands out so obviously that each expects the other to choose it.
moves.asks: What choice would two people converge on unprompted, and can I make mine that one?

moves.source: Esther Duflo, randomized field trials on poverty (Poor Economics)
moves.move: Break the grand unanswerable question into small interventions and compare each against an untouched control.
moves.asks: What is the smallest version of this I could try on some and not others to see what actually changes?

moves.source: Fei Xiaotong, From the Soil: the 'differential mode of association' in rural China
moves.move: Map relationships as ripples spreading from a person outward, with obligations shrinking with distance, rather than as fixed groups.
moves.asks: Who sits in each ring around this person, and what is owed or shared at each distance?

moves.source: Octavia Hill, Victorian housing reform through personal rent collection and tenant visits
moves.move: Pair any physical improvement with a continuing personal relationship, so care is carried by someone who knows the occupants.
moves.asks: Who will know the people here by name and keep showing up after the building work is done?

moves.source: Saul Alinsky, Rules for Radicals: tactics inside your people's experience, outside the opponent's
moves.move: Choose actions your own side already knows how to do confidently that the other side has no playbook for.
moves.asks: What can my people do well that the obstacle has never prepared for?

moves.source: Mohandas Gandhi, the 1930 Salt March
moves.move: Boil a vast principle down to one tiny everyday act that anyone can join and that cannot be ignored.
moves.asks: What is the smallest ordinary act that carries the whole idea and invites everyone to take part?

moves.source: Mary Parker Follett, Creative Experience (1924): integrative conflict resolution, as in opening a window in the next room
moves.move: Instead of splitting the difference, uncover what each side actually needs underneath its demand, so one solution serves both fully.
moves.asks: What does each party really want beneath what they asked for, and is there a way to give all of it?

moves.source: Ursula Franklin, The Real World of Technology: holistic versus prescriptive technologies
moves.move: Ask whether a design leaves the maker in control of the whole job, or splits the job into steps dictated by someone else.
moves.asks: Does this give the person the whole craft, or does it only let them follow instructions?

moves.source: Donella Meadows, 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System'
moves.move: Rank possible interventions by how deeply they act, from tweaking numbers up through information flows and rules to the goal itself.
moves.asks: Am I adjusting a number, or changing who knows what, what the rules are, or what the goal is?

moves.source: Stafford Beer, the Viable System Model and Project Cybersyn
moves.move: Let each level absorb all the variety it can handle itself and send upward only the signals it cannot absorb.
moves.asks: What can the lowest level decide alone, so the top only hears about what truly exceeds it?

moves.source: Mariana Mazzucato, The Entrepreneurial State and mission-oriented innovation
moves.move: Set one concrete, ambitious mission and let many different unplanned projects across fields contribute toward it.
moves.asks: What single hard, specific goal could many unrelated efforts each take a piece of?

moves.source: Shigeru Ban, paper-tube emergency shelters and the Cardboard Cathedral
moves.move: Pick a cheap, overlooked, locally available material and test it until it proves it can carry the load.
moves.asks: Which ordinary thing nobody respects could do this structural job if I tested it hard?

moves.source: Mozi, the siege debate with Gongshu Ban: settling a dispute with a model of attack and defense
moves.move: Resolve a disagreement by staging a miniature of both sides, one attacking and one defending, until a clear winner shows.
moves.asks: Can I build a small model of the contest and let each side play it out before committing?

moves.source: Fazlur Rahman Khan, the tube structural system for skyscrapers
moves.move: Move the strength to the outer skin so the whole envelope works together, freeing the interior from carrying the load.
moves.asks: What if the outside did the structural work and the inside were left open?

moves.source: Fannie Lou Hamer's Freedom Farm Cooperative 'pig bank' in Sunflower County, Mississippi (1969)
moves.move: Lend out a living asset that multiplies, and have each borrower repay with its offspring so the stock passes on to the next family.
moves.asks: What could I give that makes more of itself, so each person who receives it can pass some on?

moves.source: Ella Baker's group-centered leadership at the founding of SNCC (Shaw University, 1960)
moves.move: Grow many local leaders who can act without you, instead of one strong figure everyone waits on.
moves.asks: If the central person vanished tomorrow, who could already carry this on, and how do I make more of them?

moves.source: Garrett Morgan's three-position traffic signal patent (1923), with an all-directions stop between go phases
moves.move: Insert a brief state where everything halts between two conflicting flows, so the switch never catches anyone halfway across.
moves.asks: Where does this flip abruptly from one mode to another, and what pause between them would keep someone from getting caught?

moves.source: Madam C. J. Walker training thousands of Black women as commissioned 'Walker agents' (1910s)
moves.move: Turn customers into trained sellers who earn from every sale, so your growth and their income rise together.
moves.asks: Who already uses this and could earn a living by teaching it to others?

moves.source: Ida B. Wells compiling lynching statistics from white newspapers' own reports in The Red Record (1895)
moves.move: Build the case only from the other side's own published records, so they cannot wave the evidence away as yours.
moves.asks: What does the opposing side's own data already show, if I read it closely?

moves.source: The Montgomery Improvement Association's volunteer car pool during the bus boycott (1955-56)
moves.move: Replace the service you are refusing with a volunteer network of pickup points, so the refusal can last as long as it needs to.
moves.asks: If everyone stopped using the current way tomorrow, what parallel network would keep them moving?

moves.source: DJ Kool Herc's 'Merry-Go-Round', looping a record's drum break across two turntables at Bronx parties (1973)
moves.move: Find the few seconds people respond to most and extend them, looping that part instead of playing the whole.
moves.asks: Which small part makes people light up, and what if it were stretched into the main event?

moves.source: Zora Neale Hurston returning to Eatonville, Florida, to collect folklore with 'the spy-glass of Anthropology' (Mules and Men, 1935)
moves.move: Go back to the place you know from the inside and study it with an outsider's instruments, to see what familiarity hid.
moves.asks: What would I notice about my own home ground if I studied it like a stranger with a notebook?

moves.source: The Black Panther Party's Free Breakfast for Children Program, begun in Oakland (1969)
moves.move: Meet a daily need nobody else is meeting, in plain view and for free, so the service makes the argument for you.
moves.asks: What everyday need could I meet in public that would prove the point better than any speech?

moves.source: A story told of Benjamin Banneker, said to have carved a wooden clock after studying a borrowed pocket watch (c. 1753)
moves.move: Study one borrowed working example closely, then rebuild it larger from the materials you have.
moves.asks: What working example could I borrow, understand completely and rebuild from what is already here?

moves.source: Mary McLeod Bethune founding her Daytona school with $1.50 and five girls, funded by selling sweet potato pies (1904)
moves.move: Start the institution at the smallest size that works, and grow it on what it can earn from the first day.
moves.asks: What could I start this week with almost no money, paid for by something I can make and sell now?

moves.source: Dorothy Vaughan teaching herself and her West Area Computing staff FORTRAN as IBM machines arrived at NASA Langley (1961)
moves.move: When a new machine threatens your team's work, learn its language first and teach your people, so they become the ones who run it.
moves.asks: What tool is coming that could replace what we do, and how could we master it before anyone else?

moves.source: Septima Clark's Citizenship Schools on Johns Island, South Carolina, first taught by a local beautician rather than a certified teacher (1957)
moves.move: Recruit the teacher from the learners' own neighbors rather than from the credentialed experts.
moves.asks: Who among the people themselves could teach this, because they are trusted and nothing like an expert?

moves.source: Maggie Lena Walker's St. Luke Penny Savings Bank in Richmond, Virginia (1903)
moves.move: Lower the price of entry to the smallest coin, so people no one has served before can become regular members.
moves.asks: What is the smallest amount someone could start with, and what if that were enough to join?

moves.source: Pullman porters carrying bundles of Robert Abbott's Chicago Defender into the South (1910s)
moves.move: Distribute through people who already travel the route for other reasons.
moves.asks: Who already goes where this needs to go, and could they carry it along?

moves.source: Victor Hugo Green, a Harlem mail carrier, compiling The Negro Motorist Green Book from readers' reports (1936-66)
moves.move: Build the map of where it is safe to go from the reports of people who have already been there.
moves.asks: Who has already travelled this route and could tell newcomers where they will be welcome?

moves.source: Harlem rent parties of the 1920s, with a piano player and a small charge at the door
moves.move: Turn a bill you cannot pay into an event people are glad to pay to attend.
moves.asks: What cost hanging over this could become a gathering people would pay to join?

moves.source: Frederick Douglass trading bread to white boys in Baltimore for reading lessons (Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845)
moves.move: Trade what you have in plenty for small lessons from people who hold the knowledge you are denied.
moves.asks: Who already knows what I need, and what small thing of mine could I trade for a lesson?

moves.source: Toni Morrison's advice to write the book you want to read, as reported from her 1981 speech to the Ohio Arts Council
moves.move: Make the thing you went looking for and could not find.
moves.asks: What have I searched for and never found, that I could make myself?

moves.source: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who could not read, creating the Cherokee syllabary (1821)
moves.move: Map the system one-to-one onto the units people already hear and say, so it can be learned in days.
moves.asks: What units do people already use without thinking, and could the whole system be built from exactly those?

moves.source: The Navajo Code Talkers of the US Marine Corps (1942-45), Diné Marines who built a code on their own language with terms such as 'tortoise' for tank
moves.move: Build your code on a language outsiders cannot read, as Diné Marines did, then add a layer of substitutions on top.
moves.asks: What knowledge do my people already hold that outsiders cannot read, and how could it protect this?

moves.source: Lakota winter counts (waniyetu wowapi), one pictograph per year painted on a hide
moves.move: Mark each period with a single image of its most memorable event, so a long history fits on one surface.
moves.asks: If each stage got only one picture, which event would stand for it?

moves.source: The spirit line (ch'ihónít'i) in many Diné rugs, which some weavers explain as an opening running from the inner pattern to the border
moves.move: Leave one deliberate line open from the center to the edge, so the finished work does not close in on its maker.
moves.asks: Where should this stay deliberately open, so that finishing it does not close it off for good?

moves.source: The Polynesian Voyaging Society's canoe Hōkūleʻa sailing from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments (1976)
moves.move: Settle an argument about whether something was possible by rebuilding it and doing it.
moves.asks: Instead of debating whether this could work, what would it take to rebuild it and try it for real?

moves.source: Dolores Huerta directing the United Farm Workers' grape boycott from New York (1968)
moves.move: When you cannot win where the power sits, move the fight to the place where the product meets its buyers.
moves.asks: Where does this reach the people whose choices the powerful depend on, and what could happen there?

moves.source: The Young Lords' Garbage Offensive in East Harlem (1969)
moves.move: Make a neglected problem impossible to ignore by moving it into the path of the people responsible for fixing it.
moves.asks: What is being quietly ignored, and where could I put it so the responsible party has to step over it?

moves.source: Luis Valdez's El Teatro Campesino actos, staged on flatbed trucks for striking farmworkers with signs naming each role (1965)
moves.move: Hang a sign on each player naming exactly what they stand for, and stage the conflict in minutes on whatever platform is there.
moves.asks: Who are the players here, and what happens if each wears a sign naming what they really represent?

moves.source: Judith Baca's Great Wall of Los Angeles, painted section by section by teams of young people (1976-84)
moves.move: Split a long public story into sections that different teams each make in the open, so the making joins them.
moves.asks: What long story could be cut into sections that different groups each make in public?

moves.source: Grace Lee Boggs and Detroit Summer, young people planting gardens on Detroit's vacant lots (1992)
moves.move: Instead of protesting what is missing, start producing it on the spot with the people around you.
moves.asks: What could we start making here ourselves, today, rather than demanding that someone else provide it?

moves.source: Larry Itliong and Filipino grape workers starting the Delano strike, then asking the Mexican American farmworkers' union to join (1965)
moves.move: Start the action yourself, then invite the larger group to join, instead of waiting for them to lead.
moves.asks: What could I start now and then ask others to join, instead of waiting for permission?

moves.source: Maya Lin's Vietnam Veterans Memorial, listing the names in the order they died (1982)
moves.move: Order the entries by when they happened rather than alphabetically, so reading the list means reliving the sequence.
moves.asks: What if this were arranged by when things happened rather than by name or size?

moves.source: Ruth Asawa's flour, salt and water 'baker's clay' for San Francisco schoolchildren (Alvarado School Arts Workshop, 1968)
moves.move: Pick a material so cheap and forgiving that anyone can start making with it immediately.
moves.asks: What dirt-cheap, forgiving material would let everyone start making right now?

moves.source: The 1946 Hawaiʻi sugar strike, where the ILWU united Filipino, Japanese, Chinese, Native Hawaiian and Portuguese workers whom plantations had housed in separate camps
moves.move: Where those in charge keep groups apart, organize across the very line they drew.
moves.asks: What division between the people involved is being used against them, and what if they acted as one?

moves.source: Aboriginal Australian songlines, in which many peoples' custodians sing routes across Country that also carry law and story (sacred knowledge held by particular peoples)
moves.move: Tie knowledge to a sequence of places, each verse naming the next landmark, so that the song is also a way of knowing the path.
moves.asks: What sequence of stories would let someone recall every step just by telling it in order?

moves.source: Māori Kōhanga Reo language nests, where fluent elders care for preschoolers entirely in te reo (from 1982)
moves.move: Revive what is fading by putting its last fluent holders with the youngest learners in everyday care, with no other language allowed.
moves.asks: Who still holds this fully, and how could they spend ordinary days with the newest beginners?

moves.source: Kate Sheppard's 1893 women's suffrage petition to the New Zealand Parliament, glued into a roll some 270 metres long
moves.move: Join every individual voice into one continuous physical object, so its sheer size makes the argument.
moves.asks: What could I gather into a single object whose size alone shows how many people care?

moves.source: Chinua Achebe on the proverb that the hunt is told to glorify the hunter until the lions have their own historians (Paris Review, 1994)
moves.move: Retell the story from the side that has never had its own historian.
moves.asks: Who in this has never told their side, and what changes when they tell it?

moves.source: Leymah Gbowee and the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace blocking the doors of the Accra peace talks (2003)
moves.move: Gather physically at the decision-makers' doors and stay there until they decide.
moves.asks: Where do the people who must decide this actually sit, and what if they could not leave without an answer?

moves.source: Kenneth Nnebue, an electronics trader with surplus blank tapes, releasing Living in Bondage straight to VHS (1992)
moves.move: Make it fast and cheap for a channel your audience already owns, and let the volume of releases teach you what works.
moves.asks: What could I release within a week through a channel people already use, and what would ten releases teach me?

moves.source: Nelson Mandela on the regent at Mqhekezweni, who heard everyone out at tribal meetings and spoke only at the end (Long Walk to Freedom, 1994)
moves.move: Let the person with the most authority speak last, after everyone else has spoken freely.
moves.asks: What would I hear if the most powerful voice in the room went last?

moves.source: Kele talking drums of the Congo, documented by John F. Carrington in The Talking Drums of Africa (1949)
moves.move: Wrap each key word in a longer stock phrase, so the message survives a noisy channel that drops detail.
moves.asks: If this had to travel through noise, what added redundancy would keep its meaning from being mistaken?

moves.source: Chilean arpilleras, scrap-cloth scenes stitched by women relatives of the disappeared and sold abroad through the Vicaría de la Solidaridad (1970s)
moves.move: Carry a dangerous truth inside a humble craft object that can travel where speech is blocked.
moves.asks: What ordinary object could carry this message past the people who would stop it?

moves.source: Porto Alegre's participatory budgeting, in which neighborhood assemblies decide part of the city's investment budget (from 1989)
moves.move: Hand a real slice of the budget to the people affected and let them decide it in open assemblies.
moves.asks: Which part of the resources could the people affected decide directly?

moves.source: Argentina's worker-recovered factories after the 2001 crisis, run under the slogan 'occupy, resist, produce'
moves.move: When the owners walk away, let the people who know the work keep it running themselves.
moves.asks: If the people at the top left, how could those who do the work run it on their own?

moves.source: Carolina Maria de Jesus's diary of São Paulo favela life, written in notebooks she found while collecting paper (Quarto de Despejo, 1960)
moves.move: Keep a plain daily record from inside the hardship, in your own words, because it reaches people that outside reports cannot.
moves.asks: What would a daily diary kept by the person living this show that no outside report has?

moves.source: The Chipko movement in Uttarakhand, including Gaura Devi and the women of Reni holding the trees to stop the felling (1974)
moves.move: Put your own body between the threat and the thing you protect, so harming it means harming you in public.
moves.asks: What would it look like to stand physically between this and what threatens it?

moves.source: Zaha Hadid painting her early projects, such as The Peak competition entry (1983), instead of only drafting them
moves.move: Explore the design in a different medium that shows what your usual tools cannot.
moves.asks: What other medium could I sketch this in to reveal shapes my usual tools hide?

moves.source: A story told about Savitribai Phule carrying a spare sari to her girls' school in Pune after being pelted on the way (1840s)
moves.move: Expect the predictable attack and carry the remedy with you, so it costs minutes instead of the mission.
moves.asks: What will people reliably throw at this, and what spare could I carry so it barely slows me down?

moves.source: Maria Sibylla Merian, Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium (1705), drawing each insect through its life stages on its host plant
moves.move: Show the subject at every stage of its life together with what it lives on, on a single page.
moves.asks: What would I learn by drawing this across its whole life cycle, alongside what feeds it?

moves.source: Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (1966), on dirt as matter out of place
moves.move: Treat whatever people call mess or dirt as a sign of a boundary crossed, and map the order it offends.
moves.asks: What is considered out of place here, and what hidden order does that reveal?

moves.source: The Rani ki Vav stepwell in Patan, Gujarat, commissioned by Queen Udayamati (11th century)
moves.move: Build access at every level, so the resource can be reached whether it stands high or low.
moves.asks: How could people reach this whether the supply is high or low?

moves.source: Kaoru Ishikawa's cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram for quality control
moves.move: Draw the problem as a spine with a branch for each category of cause, and fill every branch before choosing one.
moves.asks: Which whole categories of cause have I not even listed yet?

moves.source: Noriaki Kano's model of quality (1984): must-be, one-dimensional and attractive qualities
moves.move: Sort every feature into those whose absence angers, those that please in proportion, and those that delight only when present.
moves.asks: What here is simply expected, what is more-is-better, and what would delight because nobody expects it?

moves.source: The Mongolian ger, whose khana lattice walls fold up like scissors when camp moves
moves.move: Make the structure collapse flat by its own geometry, so moving it costs less than staying put.
moves.asks: How could this fold for travel and spring back without losing its strength?

moves.source: Gabriel García Márquez on learning from his grandmother to tell the fantastic with a straight face (Paris Review, 1981)
moves.move: Present the strangest part in a completely flat, matter-of-fact voice, so the listener accepts it as ordinary.
moves.asks: What if the most unlikely part of this were presented as the most ordinary thing in the world?

moves.source: Michel de Montaigne's Essais (1580), each an 'essai', a trial of his own judgment
moves.move: Write a short attempt at the question with no conclusion required, then another, and let the attempts accumulate.
moves.asks: What would three short, unfinished attempts at this teach me before I commit to an answer?

moves.source: George Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), on finding a related problem you can solve
moves.move: When the problem resists, solve an easier related one first and use it as a stepping stone.
moves.asks: What easier version of this could I solve today, and what would it teach me about the real one?

moves.source: Nise da Silveira's painting studio at the Engenho de Dentro psychiatric hospital in Rio de Janeiro, opened as an alternative to electroshock (1946)
moves.move: Replace the forceful intervention with a medium through which people can show you what is going on inside.
moves.asks: What medium could let the people involved show me what they cannot tell me?

moves.source: Bilquis and Abdul Sattar Edhi's cradles outside Edhi Foundation centers in Pakistan, where babies can be left with no questions asked
moves.move: Place a safe, no-questions-asked drop point exactly where the desperate act would otherwise happen.
moves.asks: Where are people being pushed into a terrible choice, and what no-questions alternative could sit right there?

moves.source: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which granted amnesty only in exchange for full disclosure (1995 Act)
moves.move: Offer a pardon in exchange for the complete truth, so people have more reason to tell everything than to hide it.
moves.asks: What could I offer in exchange for full disclosure that would be worth more to people than staying silent?

moves.source: Jane Austen's 1816 letter on the 'little bit (two inches wide) of ivory' she worked with a fine brush
moves.move: Work on a deliberately tiny canvas with great precision instead of a broad one.
moves.asks: What if I shrank the scope to a few people or one small setting and got it exactly right?

moves.source: Elena Ferrante publishing under a pseudonym and staying out of public view since her first novel (1992)
moves.move: Separate the work from its maker entirely, so it is judged only on itself.
moves.asks: What would change about this if no one knew who made it?

moves.source: Frida Kahlo painting self-portraits in bed with a mirror fixed to its canopy after her 1925 bus accident
moves.move: When you are confined, make the confinement your vantage point and what you can see from it your subject.
moves.asks: If I could not leave this spot, what could I make from exactly what is visible from here?

moves.source: Elena Poniatowska's La noche de Tlatelolco (1971), assembled from eyewitness testimony with no narrator
moves.move: Build the account entirely from many witnesses' own words, with no single narrator stitching them together.
moves.asks: What if this were told only in the voices of the people who were there?

moves.source: Javanese batik, where hot wax protects areas of the cloth before each dye bath
moves.move: Mask off the parts that must stay as they are before you apply the change to everything else.
moves.asks: What must stay untouched, and how could I protect it before changing the rest?

constraints.text: Cut it to half the parts, steps or features you planned, and it must still do the job.
It has to work fully for someone who cannot see it.
It must be usable or makeable with one hand.
The first working version has to exist within four hours.
Use only materials, parts or code already within reach right now.
An eight-year-old must be able to explain how it works after trying it once.
It must work with no electricity, signal or network.
It must still work after being dropped, misused or ignored for a month.
It must communicate everything without a single written or spoken word.
The whole thing must fit in a pocket or on a single page.
It must keep working for fifty years with no maintenance.
Use only one material, one language or one tool.
The person using it gives it only ten seconds of attention.
A stranger must be able to build it from your instructions alone, with you absent.
Ten people must be able to use it at the same moment without taking turns.
The whole thing must cost less than the smallest banknote in your local currency.
The people who benefit must fund it entirely themselves, with no donor, grant or loan.
It must be fully usable by someone who is walking and cannot stop or put anything down.
Anyone must be able to start using it in the time it takes a kettle to boil.
Every material must be something that would otherwise have been thrown away.
It must make no sound at all, and must not depend on anyone hearing anything.
It must be fully usable by someone wearing thick winter gloves.
The only audience is one specific elderly person who distrusts anything new, and they must choose to keep it.
The people it is for must begin out of the room, sceptical, and want nothing to do with it.
It must work identically for five people and for fifty thousand without being redesigned.
It must survive a full day with a determined two-year-old and be unharmed.
It must look better after ten years of wear than on its first day.
Nobody present may ever be picked, ranked, eliminated or left waiting.
It must work in a room where phones, screens and cameras are forbidden.
The entire explanation must be a single physical gesture, with no words.
It must be completely reversible, leaving no trace that it ever existed.
It must work entirely inside a lift in the time between two floors.
It must work while soaked in heavy rain, or fully underwater.
No straight line, flat surface or right angle may appear anywhere in it.
No one may own, sell or control it, and anyone must be free to copy or alter it.
Nothing living, including plants and insects, may be harmed in making or using it.
If used completely wrongly, by the worst possible person, it must still hurt nobody.
No one may be asked to remember a password, rule, name or number.
It must work without learning who anyone is: no names, accounts, faces or tracking.
The people who will use it must make every part of it themselves.
It must be makeable by two people who cannot speak to each other.
Making it must require no tool sharper or more powerful than a spoon.
Its whole useful life lasts only ten seconds, and that moment must be unforgettable.
Every use must leave it more useful to the next person than before.
It must function when the person using it is completely alone and nobody can help.
It must be deliberately ugly in one obvious way that people still come to love.
It must be built using only techniques from a craft that has nothing to do with this problem.
It may rearrange, rename or reuse existing things, but must make nothing new.
It may communicate only through smell and touch, with nothing seen or heard.
All of it must happen within a single square metre of floor.
It must work for a traveller in a country whose language, money and customs they do not know.
When it fails, which it will, the failure must make everyone laugh rather than leave anyone worse off.
No money may change hands at any point in making or using it.
It must work in 45°C heat in full sun, with no shade or cooling.
It must be designed first for a village with no road access, and only then adapted for a city.
It must be made together with a rival or competitor, and both must come out ahead.
No one trained in this field may take part in making it.
Anyone must be able to repair it with common tools and no manual.
It must work equally well, at the same moment, for an eighty-year-old and an eight-year-old.
Everything needed to use it must fit into a song or rhyme someone can sing from memory.
